events.title: Accession of Antoninus Pius
events.summary: Titus Aurelius Antoninus, a wealthy 51-year-old senator from a family of Nemausus, succeeded Hadrian, secured his deification against senatorial resistance, and received the name Pius. In 23 years of rule he never left Italy.
events.detail: The Historia Augusta offers several explanations for 'Pius': his devotion to Hadrian, his support of his aged father-in-law in the Senate, or his saving of senators Hadrian had condemned. His reign, the longest since Augustus, is almost without narrative history: Dio's account is lost except for fragments and the Historia Augusta life is brief. Aelius Aristides's oration To Rome and the later image of the Antonine age as the happiest in human history (Gibbon) derive from it.

events.title: Death of Faustina the Elder; the puellae Faustinianae
events.summary: Annia Galeria Faustina, wife of Antoninus, died in late 140 and was deified. Antoninus founded an alimentary charity for girls in her name, the puellae Faustinianae, and built her a temple in the Forum, later dedicated to both of them.
events.detail: The Temple of Antoninus and Faustina survives as the church of San Lorenzo in Miranda, its porch columns still bearing grooves from failed medieval attempts to pull them down. Huge coin issues for DIVA FAVSTINA continued for years, among the most abundant of the period.
events.locName: Temple of Antoninus and Faustina, Forum Romanum

events.title: Construction of the Antonine Wall
events.summary: Antoninus's governor Quintus Lollius Urbicus reconquered southern Scotland and built a turf rampart on a stone base, 39 Roman miles long, across the Forth-Clyde isthmus from Bo'ness to Old Kilpatrick, with about 16-19 forts. Hadrian's Wall was largely abandoned for two decades.
events.detail: Antoninus took his only imperatorial acclamation for the victory (142), and coins of 143 show Britannia. Twenty distance slabs carved by legions II Augusta, VI Victrix and XX Valeria Victrix record the lengths each built, with reliefs of conquest and sacrifice. The advance may have been driven by Antoninus's need for military prestige rather than local necessity. The wall was abandoned around 158-165, the date being debated. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008.
scholarship: Hanson and Maxwell, Rome's North West Frontier (1983)

events.title: Marcion expelled by the Roman church
events.summary: Marcion of Sinope, a wealthy shipowner, was expelled by the church at Rome, which returned his large donation. He taught that the creator god of the Jewish scriptures was distinct from the good God revealed by Jesus, and compiled the first Christian canon: an edited Luke and ten letters of Paul.
events.detail: Tertullian dates the break 115 years and six and a half months after Christ's appearance under Tiberius. Marcionite churches spread across the empire and survived in the East for centuries. The challenge accelerated the formation of the orthodox New Testament canon and the Church's retention of the Old Testament.

events.title: Aelius Aristides delivers the Oration to Rome
events.summary: The Greek orator Publius Aelius Aristides of Smyrna delivered in Rome his panegyric To Rome, presenting the empire as a single city embracing the whole world, governed by law, open to talent, and guarded by an army on its frontiers like a wall around a city.
events.detail: It is the fullest statement of the ideology of the Antonine peace from a provincial Greek perspective, praising the extension of citizenship and the security of travel. Aristides also wrote the Sacred Tales, an extraordinary record of his illnesses and dreams in the service of Asclepius at Pergamon. The date is probably 143 or 144, though 155 has been argued.

events.title: Antoninus's Moorish war
events.summary: Raids by Moorish tribes into Mauretania required reinforcements drawn from Spain, Pannonia, Syria and elsewhere over several years; Pausanias says Antoninus drove the Moors back to the edge of the Atlas.
events.detail: Inscriptions of vexillations and the career of commanders such as Titus Varius Clemens, procurator of Mauretania Caesariensis, document the war; little narrative survives. Moorish incursions resumed into Baetica under Marcus Aurelius.

events.title: Ptolemy's Almagest and Geography
events.summary: At Alexandria Claudius Ptolemy completed the Mathematike Syntaxis (later called the Almagest), the definitive geocentric model of the universe with tables for predicting planetary positions, and the Geography, listing coordinates for some 8,000 places.
events.detail: Ptolemy's observations are dated between 127 and 141, and a 'Canobic inscription' of 147/148 recorded his parameters. The Almagest remained authoritative in the Islamic world and Europe until Copernicus; the Geography, rediscovered in the West around 1400, shaped Renaissance cartography and Columbus's underestimate of the globe. His Tetrabiblos systematised astrology, which was taken seriously at court.

events.title: Justin Martyr's First Apology
events.summary: Justin, a philosopher from Flavia Neapolis in Samaria teaching in Rome, addressed an apology for the Christians to Antoninus Pius and his adopted sons, arguing that Christians should not be punished for the name alone and that Christianity was the true philosophy.
events.detail: It contains the earliest detailed description of Christian worship: Sunday gatherings with readings from 'the memoirs of the apostles', prayers, and the eucharist of bread and wine mixed with water. Justin was beheaded around 165 under the city prefect Quintus Junius Rusticus, Marcus Aurelius's Stoic teacher; the trial record survives as the Acts of Justin.

events.title: Martyrdom of Polycarp
events.summary: Polycarp, the aged bishop of Smyrna and reputed disciple of the apostle John, was arrested during a festival, refused to swear by the emperor's genius, declaring 'Eighty-six years I have served him and he has done me no wrong', and was burned in the stadium.
events.detail: The Martyrdom of Polycarp, a letter of the church of Smyrna, is the earliest Christian martyr-act and establishes the cult of relics and the anniversary commemoration. Its date is disputed between about 155-156 and 167 (Eusebius). It shows persecution as local and crowd-driven, within the framework of Trajan's rescript.

events.title: Withdrawal from the Antonine Wall
events.summary: Within two decades of its construction the Antonine Wall was abandoned and Hadrian's Wall recommissioned. Pausanias mentions a war against the Brigantes, who were deprived of land, possibly the context for a temporary withdrawal c. 155-158.
events.detail: Older views posited two Antonine occupations separated by a gap; most now favour a single occupation ending c. 158-165, perhaps when Marcus and Verus needed troops for the East. Building inscriptions of 158 on Hadrian's Wall attest refurbishment under the governor Julius Verus.
scholarship: Hodgson, 'Were there two Antonine occupations of Scotland?', Britannia 26 (1995)
events.debate: Date and number of Antonine occupations.

events.title: Gaius's Institutes
events.summary: The jurist Gaius, otherwise almost unknown, wrote an elementary textbook of Roman law in four books arranged by persons, things and actions. It is the only classical legal work to survive substantially intact.
events.detail: Barthold Georg Niebuhr discovered it in 1816 in the Chapter Library of Verona as a palimpsest beneath letters of Jerome; papyrus fragments from Oxyrhynchus and Antinoopolis have since filled gaps. Its scheme was adopted by Justinian's Institutes (533) and through them by modern civil codes. It preserves much on Republican procedure (legis actiones, formulary system) and Augustan status law.

events.title: Death of Antoninus Pius
events.summary: Antoninus died at his estate at Lorium, aged 74, after eating Alpine cheese too greedily. In a fever he gave the tribune of the guard the watchword 'aequanimitas' and had the golden statue of Fortune transferred to Marcus's bedroom.
events.detail: He left a treasury surplus of 2,700 million sesterces, according to Dio. Marcus's long tribute to his adoptive father in the Meditations (1.16) describes his patience, courtesy and diligence. The column base of Antoninus, with its apotheosis relief, survives in the Vatican.

events.title: Joint accession of Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus
events.summary: Marcus Aurelius insisted that the Senate grant his adoptive brother Lucius the same powers and title of Augustus, creating for the first time two equal emperors. They promised the praetorians 20,000 sesterces each.
events.detail: Marcus married his daughter Lucilla to Lucius. The collegiate principate became a model for later divisions of imperial power (Diocletian's tetrarchy). Though formally equal, Marcus held the office of pontifex maximus and the greater authority.

events.title: Battle of Elegeia
events.summary: The Parthian king Vologases IV invaded Armenia and installed his own candidate. Marcus Sedatius Severianus, governor of Cappadocia, marched in with a legion, was surrounded at Elegeia on the upper Euphrates, and after three days killed himself; his army was massacred.
events.detail: Lucian says Severianus had been encouraged by the oracle of the false prophet Alexander of Abonuteichos, and mocks a historian who described his death absurdly. Dio's epitome confirms the destruction of a legion with its officers; whether it was IX Hispana, XXII Deiotariana or another is debated. A second Parthian army then defeated the governor of Syria.

battle.significance: Triggered the eastern war of Lucius Verus.

events.title: Statius Priscus takes Artaxata
events.summary: Marcus Statius Priscus, transferred from Britain, invaded Armenia, took and destroyed Artaxata, and built a new capital, Kaine Polis, with a Roman garrison. Lucius Verus took the title Armeniacus.
events.detail: Sohaemus, a Roman senator of royal Emesene and Arsacid descent, was installed as king of Armenia (coins of 164: REX ARMENIIS DATVS). Kaine Polis is identified with Vagharshapat (Echmiadzin), later the seat of the Armenian church.

events.title: Avidius Cassius sacks Seleucia and Ctesiphon
events.summary: Avidius Cassius advanced down the Euphrates, then crossed to the Tigris, where the great Hellenistic city of Seleucia received the Romans as friends but was sacked and burned; the Parthian palace at Ctesiphon was destroyed.
events.detail: Eutropius claims 400,000 inhabitants were captured. Roman sources blamed the city's alleged treachery; the Historia Augusta blames Cassius. Ammianus and the Historia Augusta tell that soldiers opening a gold chest (or crack) in the temple of Apollo released a pestilential vapour that spread plague across the empire, a moralising tale attached to the outbreak of the Antonine Plague among the returning army.

sides.losses: light in battle; heavy later to plague

battle.significance: Destroyed the greatest Greek city of Mesopotamia; associated in tradition with the origin of the Antonine Plague.

events.title: The Antonine Plague
events.summary: An epidemic that broke out in the Roman army in Mesopotamia around 165 reached Rome in 166 and swept the empire for over a decade, with a severe recurrence in 189. Galen's description of fever, diarrhoea and a black pustular rash makes smallpox the most likely identification.
events.detail: Mortality estimates range from about 10% of the population (Duncan-Jones) to a quarter or more (Scheidel, Harper). Evidence includes Egyptian papyri showing villages such as Soknopaiou Nesos losing a third to a half of their taxpayers, an abrupt halt in the gold-mining contracts at Alburnus Maior in 167, disruption of brick production and monumental building, and apotropaic oracles of Clarian Apollo inscribed in cities from Hierapolis to Hadrian's Wall. Galen fled Rome in 166 but was recalled to the army at Aquileia in 168. The plague weakened Rome's capacity to fight the Marcomannic Wars, and Marcus himself may have died of it. Dio reports 2,000 deaths a day in Rome in 189.
scholarship: Duncan-Jones, 'The impact of the Antonine plague', JRA 9 (1996)
events.debate: Disease identity and mortality; how far the plague, rather than war, caused the stresses of the late second century.

events.title: Parthian triumph of Marcus and Verus
events.summary: Marcus and Lucius celebrated a joint triumph for the Parthian war, taking the titles Armeniacus, Parthicus Maximus and Medicus. Marcus's sons Commodus (aged five) and Annius Verus were made Caesars.
events.detail: Lucian's How to Write History, written during the war, satirises the many historians who rushed to celebrate it with Thucydidean pastiche and absurd exaggeration. The returning troops brought the plague to Italy and the western provinces.

events.title: Raising of legions II and III Italica
events.summary: In anticipation of war on the Danube, Marcus Aurelius raised two new legions in Italy, II Italica and III Italica; they were later stationed in Noricum (Lauriacum) and Raetia (Castra Regina), provinces that had never had legions before.
events.detail: The foundation inscription of the fortress at Castra Regina (Regensburg), dated 179, survives. Raising legions in Italy, rather than in the provinces, was by then exceptional. Raetia and Noricum were upgraded to provinces governed by legionary legates of praetorian rank.
events.locName: Castra Regina (Regensburg), later base of III Italica

events.title: Langobardi and Obii cross the Danube
events.summary: Six thousand Langobardi and Obii crossed the Danube into Pannonia and were destroyed by cavalry under Vindex and infantry under Candidus. Eleven tribes then sent envoys, led by the Marcomannic king Ballomar, to the governor Iallius Bassus to make peace.
events.detail: This episode, preserved in a fragment of Dio, is usually taken as the opening of the Marcomannic Wars. Its significance lies in showing peoples from the lower Elbe on the Danube, a sign of pressure building in barbaricum, perhaps linked to Gothic movements towards the Black Sea.

battle.significance: First of the incursions that grew into the Marcomannic Wars.

events.title: Death of Lucius Verus
events.summary: Returning from Aquileia to Rome with Marcus, Lucius Verus suffered a stroke in his carriage near Altinum and died three days later, aged 38. Marcus became sole emperor.
events.detail: Rumours accused Marcus, Faustina and Lucilla of poisoning him, which modern scholars dismiss. Marcus deified him. The Historia Augusta paints Verus as a pleasure-loving foil to Marcus, though the letters of Fronto show a cultured and affectionate younger brother.

events.title: Marcus auctions the palace treasures
events.summary: To finance the war without new taxes, Marcus held a two-month auction in the Forum of Trajan of imperial furniture, gold and crystal goblets, statues, paintings, and Faustina's silk and gold-embroidered robes and jewels.
events.detail: Afterwards he offered to buy back items from purchasers who wished to return them. He also recruited slaves (voluntarii), gladiators (obsequentes), Dalmatian and Dardanian brigands and Greek police (diogmitae), and hired Germans to fight Germans, measures that show the manpower crisis caused by war and plague. The silver content of the denarius was cut to about 79%.

events.title: Marcomanni and Quadi invade Italy; siege of Aquileia
events.summary: After a major Roman offensive across the Danube failed with heavy losses (Lucian gives 20,000 killed), the Marcomanni and Quadi broke through the Pannonian frontier, crossed the Julian Alps, destroyed Opitergium and besieged Aquileia, the first invasion of Italy since the Cimbri.
events.detail: The praetorian prefect Furius Victorinus was killed. Ammianus says Aquileia was besieged and Opitergium destroyed. Lucian reports that on the advice of Alexander of Abonuteichos two lions were thrown into the Danube before the offensive; they swam across and were clubbed to death by the Germans. Marcus Claudius Fronto, governor of the three Dacias and Upper Moesia, was killed fighting about the same time. Tiberius Claudius Pompeianus and the future emperor Pertinax cleared the invaders from Italy and Noricum.

battle.significance: First barbarian invasion of Italy in nearly three centuries; a profound shock to the Antonine order.

events.title: Costoboci raid Greece; Moors invade Baetica
events.summary: In 170 or 171 the Costoboci from north of Dacia raided through Moesia, Thrace and Macedonia into Achaea, sacking the sanctuary of Eleusis. In 171-172 Moorish raiders crossed into Baetica and besieged Singilia Barba and threatened Italica.
events.detail: Aelius Aristides lamented the burning of Eleusis in a speech; Pausanias records that at Elatea the Olympic victor Mnesibulus died fighting the raiders. In Spain, Baetica was temporarily transferred from senatorial to imperial control, displacing the young quaestor Septimius Severus to Sardinia. The simultaneous crises show how stretched imperial defences had become.

events.title: Revolt of the Bucoli in Egypt
events.summary: The 'herdsmen' (Boukoloi) of the Nile Delta marshes, led by a priest named Isidorus, rose, defeated Roman troops and nearly captured Alexandria; Avidius Cassius, sent from Syria, suppressed them by dividing their forces.
events.detail: Dio reports that some, disguised as women, lured a centurion into a trap, sacrificed his companion and ate his entrails. The marsh-dwelling Boukoloi were a literary topos in Greek novels (Achilles Tatius, Heliodorus), but the revolt appears real, perhaps fuelled by plague, tax burdens and depopulation in the Delta.

events.title: The Rain Miracle
events.summary: A Roman force surrounded by the Quadi and dying of thirst under the summer sun was saved by a sudden downpour, while hail and lightning struck the enemy, enabling a Roman victory. The Column of Marcus shows a winged rain god streaming water over the soldiers.
events.detail: Dio's epitome attributes the miracle to the Egyptian priest Arnouphis invoking Hermes Aerios; Xiphilinus, the Byzantine epitomator, adds a Christian version: the prayers of Christian soldiers of legio XII Fulminata, a story told earlier by Apollinaris of Hierapolis and Tertullian, who cites a (spurious) letter of Marcus. Coins of 172-173 with Mercury may commemorate it. The date (172 or 174) and its relation to a separate 'lightning miracle' shown earlier on the Column are debated.

sides.strength: Field army, including legio XII Fulminata in the Christian version

battle.significance: Became a classic of both pagan and Christian claims to divine favour.

scholarship: Kovács, Marcus Aurelius' Rain Miracle and the Marcomannic Wars (2009)
events.debate: Date (172 or 174), agent (Egyptian magic, Jupiter, Christian prayer), and location.

events.title: Battle on the frozen Danube
events.summary: Iazyges cavalry, pursued onto the frozen Danube, turned to fight, hoping their horses would have the advantage on the ice. The Romans formed up, braced their feet on their shields, seized the reins and shields of the enemy and dragged riders and horses down, winning the fight.
events.detail: Dio's vivid account is one of the few tactical narratives of the Marcomannic Wars. The war against the Sarmatian Iazyges continued until 175, when Marcus, preoccupied by Cassius's revolt, made peace.

battle.significance: Illustrates Roman adaptability against Sarmatian cavalry.

events.title: Revolt of Avidius Cassius
events.summary: On a false report of Marcus's death, Gaius Avidius Cassius, holding a special command over the whole East, was proclaimed emperor and recognised in Syria, Egypt and much of the East. After three months and six days he was murdered by a centurion and his head sent to Marcus.
events.detail: Dio reports a story that the empress Faustina, fearing for her son's future if Marcus died, had encouraged Cassius. Martius Verus held Cappadocia for Marcus. Marcus made peace with the Iazyges, travelled east, refused to see Cassius's head, burned his correspondence unread and pardoned most supporters. Faustina died at Halala in Cappadocia in the winter of 175/176; the village was refounded as Faustinopolis. Papyri dated by Cassius's regnal years show his recognition in Egypt. Thereafter no senator was allowed to govern his home province.

events.title: Peace with the Iazyges
events.summary: To free himself to deal with Cassius, Marcus made peace with the Iazyges under their king Zanticus. They returned 100,000 Roman captives, were barred from settling within a strip along the Danube, and supplied 8,000 cavalry, of whom 5,500 were sent to Britain.
events.detail: Sarmatian cavalry are later attested at Bremetennacum (Ribchester) in Lancashire, where a unit of Sarmatians remained into the third century. Marcus took the title Sarmaticus. The figure of 100,000 captives, even if exaggerated, shows the scale of the raids.

events.title: Marcus at Athens: initiation and chairs of philosophy
events.summary: Returning from the East, Marcus and Commodus were initiated into the Eleusinian mysteries, and Marcus endowed chairs of philosophy at Athens for the Platonic, Aristotelian, Stoic and Epicurean schools, with salaries of 10,000 drachmas, plus a chair of rhetoric.
events.detail: Philostratus says Herodes Atticus was asked to choose the holders. The endowment institutionalised Athens as the empire's university city; the chairs survived in some form until Justinian's measures against pagan teachers in 529.

events.title: German and Sarmatian triumph; Column of Marcus Aurelius
events.summary: Marcus and Commodus triumphed over the Germans and Sarmatians on 23 December 176. A column with a spiral relief of the wars, modelled on Trajan's, was erected in the Campus Martius and completed by 193.
events.detail: The column's frieze is cruder and more emotional than Trajan's: barbarians are beheaded, women and children dragged off, villages burned, and the emperor appears as a remote, frontal figure. It includes the 'rain miracle' and 'lightning miracle' scenes. An inscription of the procurator Adrastus (193) records the completion. The statue of St Paul has stood on top since 1589, and the Piazza Colonna is named after it.
scholarship: Beckmann, The Column of Marcus Aurelius (2011)

events.title: Commodus made co-Augustus
events.summary: Marcus made his 15-year-old son Commodus consul and co-Augustus with tribunician power, breaking with the century-old practice of adopting an adult successor and returning to hereditary succession.
events.detail: Marcus was the first emperor since Vespasian to have a surviving son, and there is no evidence he considered passing him over. Later writers, starting with Dio and the Historia Augusta, blamed Marcus for the choice; modern historians note that excluding a son would almost certainly have led to civil war.

events.title: Martyrs of Lyon and Vienne
events.summary: A pogrom against the Christians of Lugdunum and Vienne culminated in the trial and execution of some 48 believers, including the 90-year-old bishop Pothinus, who died in prison, and the slave woman Blandina, who survived days of torture and was finally gored by a bull in the amphitheatre.
events.detail: The letter of the churches of Vienne and Lyon to those of Asia and Phrygia, preserved by Eusebius, is a key martyr text. The governor consulted Marcus, who ruled that Roman citizens should be beheaded and those who recanted released; the citizen Attalus was nonetheless thrown to the beasts. The executions took place at the annual festival of the Three Gauls in August, possibly linked to the senatorial decree of the same year allowing priests to buy condemned criminals cheaply for shows. Irenaeus became bishop afterwards.
events.locName: Amphitheatre of the Three Gauls, Lugdunum

events.title: Senatus consultum on the cost of gladiatorial games
events.summary: On the proposal of Marcus and Commodus, the Senate capped the prices that could be charged for gladiators by class and abolished the treasury's tax on gladiatorial sales, relieving provincial high priests burdened by the obligation to give games.
events.detail: The decree survives in a bronze tablet from Italica in Spain (Aes Italicense, CIL II 6278) and a marble fragment from Sardis. It includes the speech of a senator praising the emperors and a clause allowing Gallic priests to buy condemned criminals (trinqui) at six aurei each from procurators, a detail perhaps connected to the deaths of the Lyon martyrs.
scholarship: Oliver and Palmer, 'Minutes of an act of the Roman Senate', Hesperia 24 (1955)
Carter, 'Gladiatorial combat: the rules of engagement', CJ 102 (2006)

events.title: Marcus Aurelius writes the Meditations
events.summary: During his campaigns Marcus wrote, in Greek, private notes of Stoic self-exhortation known as 'To Himself' (Ta eis heauton), now called the Meditations. Book 1 is headed 'among the Quadi on the Granua' and Book 2 'at Carnuntum'.
events.detail: The work was apparently never meant for publication; it is first mentioned by Themistius in 364 and the Byzantine scholar Arethas around 900. The first printed edition (Zurich, 1558) was based on a now-lost manuscript. Its themes (the transience of life, duty, the cosmos as a city) made it among the most widely read ancient texts in modern times.

events.title: The Laugaricio inscription
events.summary: On the castle rock at Trenčín in Slovakia, some 120 km north of the Danube, a Latin inscription records that 855 soldiers of legio II Adiutrix wintered at Laugaricio 'to the victory of the emperors' under their legate Marcus Valerius Maximianus.
events.detail: It is the northernmost Roman inscription in central Europe and direct evidence of Roman garrisons deep in Quadi territory in Marcus's second expedition. Dio says 20,000 Roman soldiers were stationed in forts among the Marcomanni and Quadi. Maximianus's career inscription from Diana Veteranorum in Numidia records that he killed Valao, king of the Naristi, with his own hand.

events.title: Death of Marcus Aurelius
events.summary: Marcus Aurelius died on campaign, at Vindobona according to Aurelius Victor or at Sirmium according to Tertullian, aged 58, possibly of the plague. Commodus, aged 18, became sole emperor.
events.detail: Dio, a contemporary, judged that with his death history descended 'from a kingdom of gold to one of iron and rust'. The Historia Augusta has him tell the tribune of the watch on the last day, 'Go to the rising sun, I am already setting'. He was deified immediately. His equestrian bronze statue, preserved because it was thought to represent Constantine, stands in the Capitoline Museums.

events.title: Commodus's peace with the Marcomanni and Quadi
events.summary: Against the advice of senior generals like Pompeianus, Commodus ended the war on terms: the Marcomanni and Quadi returned prisoners and deserters, paid annual grain and supplied weapons and recruits, were forbidden to settle near the Danube or to assemble except monthly in one place under a Roman centurion. Roman garrisons in barbaricum were withdrawn.
events.detail: Herodian portrays Commodus as eager to return to Rome's pleasures; Dio, more balanced, records the terms. Modern historians often consider the peace realistic given plague and exhaustion, and it held for decades. Marcus's intended provinces of Marcomannia and Sarmatia, if they were ever intended, were abandoned. Commodus triumphed on 22 October 180.

events.title: Conspiracy of Lucilla
events.summary: Commodus's elder sister Lucilla, widow of Lucius Verus, plotted his murder with Ummidius Quadratus and Claudius Pompeianus Quintianus. Quintianus botched the attack at the entrance to the amphitheatre by brandishing his dagger and shouting 'This is what the Senate sends you!'
events.detail: Lucilla was exiled to Capri and executed; the praetorian prefect Tarrutenius Paternus was also killed, leaving Perennis in control. The episode, in which the attacker's words implicated the Senate, permanently soured Commodus towards the senatorial order and led to his withdrawal from government into the hands of favourites.

events.title: War in northern Britain under Commodus
events.summary: Dio calls it the greatest of Commodus's wars: northern tribes crossed 'the wall separating them from the Roman forts', killed a general and his troops, and were driven back by the harsh disciplinarian Ulpius Marcellus. Commodus took the title Britannicus in 184.
events.detail: Which wall is meant (Hadrian's or the Antonine) is uncertain; destruction layers at forts such as Halton Chesters and Rudchester have been linked to this invasion. Marcellus's severity provoked the army, which tried to proclaim a legate named Priscus emperor, and sent a delegation to Rome against Perennis.

events.title: Fall of Perennis
events.summary: The praetorian prefect Sextus Tigidius Perennis, who governed while Commodus amused himself, was overthrown when a delegation of 1,500 javelin-men from the army of Britain marched to Rome and accused him of plotting to make his son emperor. Commodus surrendered him to them, and he was killed with his family.
events.detail: Dio's account of a provincial army delegation reaching the emperor near Rome is unique. Herodian gives a different version, linked to coins found showing Perennis's son. The freedman chamberlain Cleander replaced Perennis as the power behind the throne.

events.title: The 'War of the Deserters' of Maternus
events.summary: A deserter named Maternus led bands of fugitive soldiers and brigands who plundered Gaul and Spain, storming towns and freeing prisoners. He then plotted to infiltrate Rome disguised as a praetorian and kill Commodus at the festival of the Hilaria, but was betrayed and beheaded.
events.detail: Herodian is the main source and presents a romanticised story; inscriptions mention operations against 'deserters' and the legio VIII Augusta's relief of Argentorate, earning it the title Pia Fidelis Constans Commoda. The episode reflects the social dislocation left by war and plague.

events.title: Grain riot and fall of Cleander
events.summary: The freedman chamberlain Marcus Aurelius Cleander, who sold offices so freely that there were 25 consuls in a single year, was blamed for a grain shortage. A crowd at the Circus rioted, marched on Commodus at the villa of the Quintilii, and Commodus had Cleander executed and his head handed to the mob.
events.detail: Dio, an eyewitness, says the shortage was deliberately engineered by the grain prefect Papirius Dionysius to bring down Cleander. The crisis followed a recurrence of plague in 189 that killed, Dio says, up to 2,000 people a day in Rome. Commodus formed an African grain fleet, the classis Commodiana Herculea, in 186 to secure supply.
events.locName: Villa of the Quintilii, Via Appia

events.title: Commodus as Hercules; Rome renamed Colonia Commodiana
events.summary: In his last years Commodus identified himself with Hercules, renamed Rome the 'Colonia Lucia Annia Commodiana', renamed the months after his twelve names, and fought as a secutor in the arena, killing animals by the hundred.
events.detail: The month names were Lucius, Aelius, Aurelius, Commodus, Augustus, Herculeus, Romanus, Exsuperatorius, Amazonius, Invictus, Felix and Pius. Dio, as a senator in the audience, records chewing a laurel leaf to hide his laughter when Commodus advanced towards the senators brandishing the severed head of an ostrich. The famous Capitoline bust shows him with lion skin, club and the apples of the Hesperides. He replaced the head of Nero's Colossus with his own.

events.title: Fire of 192
events.summary: A fire, starting perhaps from an earthquake or lightning, destroyed the Temple of Peace, the warehouses along the Via Sacra, the temple of Vesta (from which the Palladium was rescued) and parts of the Palatine.
events.detail: Galen lost books, drugs, instruments and recipes stored in a warehouse on the Via Sacra, including his own unpublished works and rare editions of earlier authors. He described the loss in De indolentia (On Avoiding Grief), rediscovered in 2005 in a manuscript at the Vlatadon monastery in Thessaloniki. Herodian took the fire as an omen of Commodus's fall.
events.locName: Temple of Peace and Via Sacra, Rome
scholarship: Rothschild and Thompson (eds), Galen's De indolentia (2014)

events.title: Assassination of Commodus
events.summary: On the last night of 192, as Commodus planned to enter his consulship on 1 January dressed as a gladiator, his mistress Marcia, the chamberlain Eclectus and the praetorian prefect Laetus gave him poisoned food. When he vomited it, they sent the wrestler Narcissus to strangle him in his bath.
events.detail: The conspirators offered the throne to the city prefect Pertinax, who was proclaimed on 1 January 193. The Senate declared Commodus a public enemy and ordered his memory damned; Septimius Severus later rehabilitated and deified him in 195 to legitimise his own claim to be Marcus's son. Commodus's death ended the Antonine dynasty and opened the civil wars of 193.
